Relevance: Freshwater consumption per customer directly impacts operational costs, regulatory compliance, and customer engagement.
Financial Impact: Reduces water procurement costs, wastewater treatment expenses, and potential regulatory fines.
Stakeholder Perspective: Customers, investors, and regulators focus on freshwater consumption per customer as a key indicator of sustainability performance and operational efficiency.

Description: This metric measures the percentage of water-saving projects implemented within a given timeframe, demonstrating the company's proactive approach to water conservation and sustainability.
Calculation: (Number of water-saving projects implemented / Total number of water-saving projects planned) × 100
Relevance: Water-saving project implementation directly impacts water efficiency, operational costs, and sustainability performance.
Financial Impact: Reduces water procurement costs, wastewater treatment expenses, and potential regulatory fines.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and stakeholders focus on water-saving project implementation as a key indicator of sustainability performance and long-term strategy.

Description: Tracks the proportion of coal ash that is recycled and reused, indicating the company's commitment to reducing waste and environmental impact.
Calculation: (Coal ash recycled / Total coal ash generated) × 100
Relevance: Demonstrates progress towards circular economy goals and reduction of environmental liabilities.
Financial Impact: Reduces costs associated with ash disposal and generates revenue from recycled materials.
Stakeholder Perspective: Environmental groups and sustainability-focused investors value recycling and waste reduction efforts.

Description: Measures the proportion of available ash pond capacity used, indicating the need for additional storage or remediation efforts.
Calculation: (Total ash stored in ponds / Total available ash pond capacity) × 100
Relevance: Essential for assessing the operational and environmental risks associated with ash pond management.
Financial Impact: Affects costs associated with ash pond maintenance, expansion, or closure.
Stakeholder Perspective: Regulators and investors focus on environmental and operational risks.

Unit: Number of contaminated sites / Total sites monitored
Description: Tracks the incidence of groundwater contamination related to coal ash disposal, indicating the effectiveness of ash management practices.
Calculation: Number of sites with contaminated groundwater / Total number of sites monitored
Relevance: Critical for assessing environmental risks and regulatory compliance.
Financial Impact: Directly affects costs associated with remediation, regulatory penalties, and potential liabilities.
Stakeholder Perspective: Regulators, investors, and local communities focus on environmental health and safety.

Metric Name: Coal Ash Disposal Cost per Ton
Description: Measures the cost of disposing of coal ash, providing insight into the financial burden of ash management.
Calculation: Total coal ash disposal costs / Total coal ash disposed (tons)
Relevance: Essential for understanding the operational costs and financial risks associated with coal ash management.
Financial Impact: Directly affects the company's cost structure and profitability.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors and financial analysts focus on cost management and operational efficiency.

Description: Tracks the capital expenditures related to coal ash management, including investments in recycling facilities, ash pond closures, or new storage infrastructure.
Calculation: Total capital expenditures for ash management
Relevance: Indicates the company's commitment to environmental stewardship and regulatory compliance.
Financial Impact: Affects the company's capital allocation and investment priorities.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors and financial analysts evaluate the company's strategy and financial commitments to ash management.

Description: Measures the company's compliance with relevant regulations and standards for coal ash management, indicating the effectiveness of its environmental management systems.
Calculation: (Number of compliant sites / Total sites monitored) × 100
Relevance: Essential for assessing regulatory risks and environmental performance.
Financial Impact: Directly affects costs associated with regulatory penalties, fines, and compliance efforts.
Stakeholder Perspective: Regulators, investors, and local communities focus on environmental stewardship and regulatory compliance.

Description: Tracks the company's progress towards reducing coal ash generation and increasing recycling rates, indicating its commitment to long-term sustainability.
Calculation: Specific reduction target (e.g., 20% by 2025)
Relevance: Demonstrates the company's strategic commitment to environmental sustainability and coal ash management.
Financial Impact: Affects long-term costs, revenue, and profitability through reduced environmental liabilities and improved operational efficiency.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and environmental groups value forward-looking targets and strategic planning.

Description: The annual growth rate of electricity connections to underserved or off-grid communities.
Calculation: ((New connections / Existing connections) × 100) - 100
Relevance: This metric evaluates the company's efforts to expand energy access to marginalized communities.
Financial Impact: Increased revenue from new connections and enhanced social license to operate.
Stakeholder Perspective: Local communities, regulators, and investors interested in ESG performance.

Description: A measure of the variability in electricity prices, reflecting the company's ability to manage price risks and provide stable energy costs to customers.
Calculation: Standard deviation of monthly electricity prices over a 12-month period
Relevance: This metric assesses the company's risk management and pricing strategies.
Financial Impact: Price volatility can affect revenue stability and profitability.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and customers concerned about energy cost stability.

Description: The proportion of eligible low-income customers enrolled in CAPs, which provide financial assistance for energy bills.
Calculation: (CAP participants / Eligible low-income customers) × 100
Relevance: This metric evaluates the company's efforts to support vulnerable customers and promote energy affordability.
Financial Impact: CAPs can reduce bad debt and improve customer satisfaction.
Stakeholder Perspective: Low-income households, regulatory bodies, and investors focused on social responsibility.

Description: The total energy savings achieved through energy efficiency programs, such as rebates for efficient appliances or home audits.
Calculation: Total energy savings from efficiency programs (MWh)
Relevance: This metric assesses the company's commitment to reducing energy consumption and promoting energy efficiency.
Financial Impact: Energy efficiency programs can reduce energy demand, lower costs, and generate revenue through incentives.
Stakeholder Perspective: Customers, regulators, and investors interested in sustainability performance.

Description: The proportion of customers enrolled in TOU pricing plans, which can help manage peak demand and promote energy efficiency.
Calculation: (TOU pricing customers / Total customers) × 100
Relevance: This metric evaluates the company's efforts to promote energy efficiency and manage peak demand.
Financial Impact: TOU pricing can reduce peak demand, lower costs, and generate revenue through more efficient energy use.
Stakeholder Perspective: Customers, regulators, and investors interested in innovative pricing strategies.

Description: The proportion of customers with past-due balances and those disconnected for non-payment, indicating the company's effectiveness in managing credit and customer relationships.
Calculation: (Customers with past-due balances / Total customers) × 100 and (Disconnected customers / Total customers) × 100
Relevance: This metric assesses the company's credit management and customer service practices.
Financial Impact: High debt and disconnection rates can lead to increased bad debt, reputational damage, and regulatory scrutiny.
Stakeholder Perspective: Customers, regulators, and investors concerned about customer treatment and financial performance.

Description: The proportion of capital expenditures and operating expenses dedicated to initiatives promoting energy affordability, such as low-income programs and energy efficiency investments.
Calculation: (Affordability investments / Total capital expenditures and operating expenses) × 100
Relevance: This metric evaluates the company's commitment to energy affordability and social responsibility.
Financial Impact: Investments in affordability initiatives can lead to long-term cost savings, improved customer satisfaction, and enhanced social license to operate.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and customers interested in the company's social and environmental performance.

Description: Tracks the percentage of employees participating in health and wellness programs, such as mental health support, fitness initiatives, or health screenings. This metric evaluates the effectiveness of employee wellness initiatives.
Calculation: (Number of employees participating in wellness programs / Total number of employees) x 100
Relevance: Demonstrates the sector's commitment to employee well-being, which can impact productivity, absenteeism, and turnover.
Financial Impact: Can lead to reduced healthcare costs, improved employee engagement, and increased retention.
Stakeholder Perspective: Employees, investors, and customers value a healthy and supportive work environment.

Metric Name: Occupational Health and Safety Management System (OHSMS) Certification Rate
Description: Measures the percentage of employees working in areas with OHSMS certifications, such as ISO 45001. This metric assesses the sector's adherence to international health and safety standards.
Calculation: (Number of employees in certified areas / Total number of employees) x 100
Relevance: Critical for evaluating the sector's commitment to systematic health and safety management and risk reduction.
Financial Impact: Certification can reduce regulatory risks, insurance premiums, and operational costs.
Stakeholder Perspective: Regulators, investors, and customers expect adherence to international health and safety standards.

Description: Tracks the frequency of near miss incidents reported, per 200,000 hours worked. This metric encourages a proactive safety culture and identifies potential hazards.
Calculation: (Number of near misses reported / Total hours worked) x 200,000
Relevance: Essential for identifying potential safety risks and areas for improvement in safety protocols and training.
Financial Impact: Can prevent future accidents, reducing operational costs, workers' compensation claims, and regulatory fines.
Stakeholder Perspective: Employees, investors, and regulators value a proactive safety culture.

Metric Name: Return to Work (RTW) Rate after Injury or Illness
Description: Measures the percentage of employees who return to work after an injury or illness, within a specific timeframe. This metric evaluates the effectiveness of return-to-work programs.
Calculation: (Number of employees returned to work / Total number of employees with injuries or illnesses) x 100
Relevance: Critical for assessing the sector's support for employee well-being and successful return to work.
Financial Impact: Impacts workers' compensation claims, operational costs, and employee retention.
Stakeholder Perspective: Employees, investors, and regulators value effective return-to-work programs.

Metric Name: Safety Training and Development Hours per Employee
Description: Tracks the average number of safety training and development hours provided to employees per year. This metric evaluates the sector's investment in employee safety skills and knowledge.
Calculation: Total safety training and development hours / Total number of employees
Relevance: Essential for assessing the sector's commitment to employee safety skills and knowledge development.
Financial Impact: Can lead to improved safety performance, reduced accidents, and lower operational costs.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and employees value a well-trained workforce.

Description: Measures employee perceptions of the safety culture, through surveys or feedback mechanisms. This metric evaluates the effectiveness of safety leadership and employee engagement.
Calculation: Average index score from employee surveys or feedback
Relevance: Critical for assessing the sector's safety culture and employee engagement.
Financial Impact: Impacts employee retention, productivity, and overall business performance.
Stakeholder Perspective: Employees, investors, and regulators value a positive safety culture.

Metric Name: Compliance with Regulatory Health and Safety Requirements
Description: Tracks the percentage of compliance with regulatory health and safety requirements, such as OSHA standards. This metric evaluates the sector's adherence to regulatory requirements.
Calculation: (Number of compliant sites / Total number of sites) x 100
Relevance: Essential for evaluating the sector's commitment to regulatory compliance and risk management.
Financial Impact: Non-compliance can result in fines, penalties, and reputational damage.
Stakeholder Perspective: Regulators, investors, and customers expect adherence to regulatory health and safety requirements.

Description: Measures the company's ability to manage peak demand through demand response programs, which helps maintain grid stability and reduces the strain on generation and transmission infrastructure.
Calculation: Total peak demand response capacity (MW) / Total peak demand (MW) × 100
Relevance: This metric is essential for electric utilities and power generators as it indicates their ability to manage peak demand, ensure grid reliability, and mitigate potential revenue losses due to demand fluctuations.
Financial Impact: Effective peak demand management can lead to reduced generation and transmission costs, lower capacity payments, and increased revenue through demand response program offerings.
Stakeholder Perspective: Regulators, investors, and grid operators value demand response capabilities as they contribute to a more resilient and efficient energy system.

Description: Measures the company's progress in reducing customer energy consumption through energy efficiency programs, smart grid initiatives, and other demand-side management strategies.
Calculation: (Total customer energy usage in current year / Total customer energy usage in base year) × 100
Relevance: This metric is vital for electric utilities and power generators as it indicates their ability to influence customer energy usage, reduce energy demand, and capitalize on emerging market opportunities.
Financial Impact: A lower CEUI can lead to reduced energy sales, but also reduces strain on the grid, lowers energy costs, and creates opportunities for energy efficiency program offerings.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and customers value CEUI as it reflects the company's ability to manage energy demand, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and promote sustainable energy practices.

Description: Measures the company's progress in modernizing its grid infrastructure to support increased efficiency, reliability, and resilience.
Calculation: (Total grid modernization investments / Total grid infrastructure assets) × 100
Relevance: This metric is crucial for electric utilities and power generators as it indicates their ability to adapt to changing energy market conditions, integrate new technologies, and maintain grid reliability.
Financial Impact: Grid modernization can lead to reduced operational expenses, increased revenue through new services, and improved asset utilization.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and grid operators value GMI as it reflects the company's ability to maintain a reliable, efficient, and resilient grid.

Metric Name: Renewable Energy Portfolio Standard (RPS) Compliance Rate
Description: Measures the company's progress in meeting regulatory requirements for renewable energy portfolio standards, which contributes to business model resilience by reducing dependence on fossil fuels and mitigating regulatory risks.
Calculation: (Total renewable energy generation / Total energy generation) × 100
Relevance: This metric is essential for electric utilities and power generators as it indicates their ability to comply with regulatory requirements, manage renewable energy risks, and capitalize on emerging market opportunities.
Financial Impact: RPS compliance can lead to reduced regulatory risks, increased revenue through renewable energy sales, and improved brand reputation.
Stakeholder Perspective: Regulators, investors, and customers value RPS compliance as it reflects the company's commitment to sustainability, renewable energy, and greenhouse gas emissions reduction.

Metric Name: Energy Storage Capacity as a Percentage of Peak Demand
Description: Measures the company's progress in deploying energy storage technologies to support grid stability, reliability, and resilience.
Calculation: (Total energy storage capacity / Total peak demand) × 100
Relevance: This metric is vital for electric utilities and power generators as it indicates their ability to manage intermittency, ensure grid reliability, and capitalize on emerging market opportunities.
Financial Impact: Energy storage can lead to reduced generation and transmission costs, increased revenue through energy storage services, and improved asset utilization.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and grid operators value energy storage capabilities as they contribute to a more resilient and efficient energy system.

Metric Name: Smart Grid Investment as a Percentage of Total Grid Investments
Description: Measures the company's progress in investing in smart grid technologies to support increased efficiency, reliability, and resilience.
Calculation: (Total smart grid investments / Total grid investments) × 100
Relevance: This metric is crucial for electric utilities and power generators as it indicates their ability to adapt to changing energy market conditions, integrate new technologies, and maintain grid reliability.
Financial Impact: Smart grid investments can lead to reduced operational expenses, increased revenue through new services, and improved asset utilization.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and grid operators value smart grid investments as they contribute to a more efficient, reliable, and resilient energy system.

Metric Name: Customer Engagement and Energy Efficiency Program Participation Rate
Description: Measures the company's progress in engaging customers and promoting energy efficiency program participation to support reduced energy demand and increased business model resilience.
Calculation: (Total energy efficiency program participants / Total customers) × 100
Relevance: This metric is essential for electric utilities and power generators as it indicates their ability to influence customer energy usage, reduce energy demand, and capitalize on emerging market opportunities.
Financial Impact: Customer engagement and energy efficiency program participation can lead to reduced energy sales, but also reduces strain on the grid, lowers energy costs, and creates opportunities for energy efficiency program offerings.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and customers value customer engagement and energy efficiency program participation as they reflect the company's commitment to sustainability, customer satisfaction, and energy efficiency.

Description: Tracks the frequency of emergency response drills conducted by the company, including those for nuclear accidents, natural disasters, and other critical incidents. This metric evaluates the preparedness of emergency response teams.
Calculation: Number of emergency response drills conducted per year
Relevance: Assesses the company's readiness to respond to critical incidents, ensuring minimal impact on operations and stakeholders.
Financial Impact: Effective emergency response can reduce potential losses, mitigate reputational damage, and ensure regulatory compliance.
Stakeholder Perspective: Regulators, investors, and local communities value regular emergency response drills as a demonstration of the company's commitment to safety and preparedness.

Description: Measures the average radiation exposure per worker in the nuclear power generation workforce. This metric evaluates the effectiveness of radiation protection measures and worker safety protocols.
Calculation: Total radiation exposure (mSv) / Total number of workers
Relevance: Critical for ensuring worker safety, regulatory compliance, and minimizing occupational health risks.
Financial Impact: Directly affects worker compensation, health insurance costs, and potential liabilities for radiation-related illnesses.
Stakeholder Perspective: Workers, regulators, and investors prioritize worker safety and radiation protection due to its impact on health and operational performance.

Description: Evaluates the company's nuclear safety culture through surveys, audits, and assessments. This metric assesses the effectiveness of safety policies, procedures, and training programs.
Calculation: Weighted average of survey responses, audit findings, and assessment results
Relevance: Essential for identifying areas for improvement in nuclear safety culture, ensuring a proactive and safety-focused work environment.
Financial Impact: A strong safety culture can reduce incidents, improve operational efficiency, and minimize regulatory risks.
Stakeholder Perspective: Regulators, investors, and workers value a strong nuclear safety culture as a critical component of safe and reliable operations.

Description: Measures the effectiveness of offsite consequence mitigation measures, including evacuation plans, sheltering, and iodine distribution. This metric evaluates the company's preparedness for nuclear incidents with offsite consequences.
Calculation: (Number of successful mitigations / Total number of offsite consequence events) × 100
Relevance: Critical for protecting public health and safety in the event of a nuclear incident with offsite consequences.
Financial Impact: Effective offsite consequence mitigation can reduce potential liabilities, minimize reputational damage, and ensure regulatory compliance.
Stakeholder Perspective: Local communities, regulators, and investors prioritize effective offsite consequence mitigation due to its impact on public health and safety.

Metric Name: Emergency Response Training Hours per Employee
Description: Tracks the average annual emergency response training hours provided to employees involved in nuclear operations. This metric evaluates the company's investment in employee preparedness.
Calculation: Total emergency response training hours / Total number of employees
Relevance: Essential for ensuring employees are equipped to respond effectively in emergency situations, minimizing risks and consequences.
Financial Impact: Effective emergency response training can reduce operational risks, minimize regulatory fines, and protect the company's reputation.
Stakeholder Perspective: Regulators, investors, and employees value regular emergency response training as a demonstration of the company's commitment to safety and preparedness.

Description: Measures the company's compliance rate with nuclear regulatory requirements, including those related to safety, security, and environmental protection. This metric evaluates the effectiveness of regulatory compliance programs.
Calculation: (Number of compliant regulatory requirements / Total number of regulatory requirements) × 100
Relevance: Critical for ensuring safe and reliable operations, minimizing regulatory risks, and maintaining public trust.
Financial Impact: Non-compliance can result in significant fines, penalties, and reputational damage.
Stakeholder Perspective: Regulators, investors, and the general public prioritize nuclear regulatory compliance due to its impact on safety, environmental protection, and public trust.

Unit: Core damage frequency (CDF) or large early release frequency (LERF)
Description: Evaluates the company's nuclear safety performance using probabilistic safety assessments (PSAs), which estimate the likelihood of core damage or radioactive releases. This metric assesses the effectiveness of safety management and risk reduction measures.
Calculation: CDF or LERF values derived from PSA models
Relevance: Essential for identifying potential safety risks, prioritizing risk reduction measures, and ensuring safe and reliable operations.
Financial Impact: Effective risk management can reduce potential liabilities, minimize regulatory fines, and protect the company's reputation.
Stakeholder Perspective: Regulators, investors, and the general public value PSA scores as a forward-looking indicator of nuclear safety performance and risk management effectiveness.

Description: Measures the frequency of power outages, providing insight into grid reliability and maintenance effectiveness.
Calculation: Total power outages / Total customers served (× 1,000)
Relevance: A leading indicator of grid resiliency, enabling proactive maintenance and investment in grid modernization.
Financial Impact: Reduced power outages minimize revenue loss, lower operational expenses, and enhance customer satisfaction.
Stakeholder Perspective: Customers and investors prioritize grid reliability, as it affects economic productivity and quality of life.

Description: Measures the average duration of power outages, reflecting the utility's effectiveness in restoring service and maintaining grid reliability.
Calculation: Total outage duration (hours) / Total power outages
Relevance: A lagging indicator of grid resiliency, providing insight into operational performance and areas for improvement.
Financial Impact: Shorter outage durations minimize revenue loss, reduce operational expenses, and enhance customer satisfaction.
Stakeholder Perspective: Customers, investors, and regulators prioritize rapid restoration of service, as it affects economic productivity and public health.

Description: Measures the proportion of total capital expenditure dedicated to grid modernization initiatives, such as smart grid technologies and grid resilience projects.
Calculation: Grid modernization investment / Total capital expenditure (× 100)
Relevance: A forward-looking indicator of the utility's commitment to grid resiliency and long-term sustainability.
Financial Impact: Strategic investments in grid modernization can reduce operational expenses, enhance revenue growth, and mitigate regulatory risks.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors and regulators value grid modernization investments, as they enhance grid resiliency, reliability, and sustainability.

Description: Measures the average time to respond to and contain cybersecurity incidents, reflecting the utility's preparedness and resilience against cyber threats.
Calculation: Total response time (hours) / Total cybersecurity incidents
Relevance: A leading indicator of the utility's cybersecurity posture and grid resiliency.
Financial Impact: Rapid incident response minimizes potential revenue loss, reduces operational expenses, and mitigates reputational risks.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and customers prioritize robust cybersecurity measures, as they protect sensitive data and maintain grid reliability.

Description: Measures the frequency of power outages caused by severe weather events, providing insight into grid resilience and preparedness.
Calculation: Total weather-related outages / Total customers served (× 1,000)
Relevance: A leading indicator of grid resiliency, enabling proactive measures to mitigate the impact of extreme weather events.
Financial Impact: Reduced weather-related outages minimize revenue loss, lower operational expenses, and enhance customer satisfaction.
Stakeholder Perspective: Customers, investors, and regulators prioritize grid resilience in the face of climate change and extreme weather events.

Description: A composite score measuring the condition and performance of grid assets, incorporating metrics such as asset age, maintenance history, and condition assessments.
Calculation: Weighted average of:
Relevance: Provides a comprehensive view of asset health, enabling proactive maintenance and investment in grid modernization.
Financial Impact: Optimizes asset performance, reduces maintenance expenses, and extends asset lifespan.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors and regulators value asset health, as it affects grid reliability, safety, and long-term sustainability.

Description: Measures the utility's capital expenditure dedicated to grid resiliency initiatives, such as grid modernization, storm hardening, and cybersecurity enhancements.
Calculation: Total capital expenditure on grid resiliency initiatives
Relevance: A forward-looking indicator of the utility's commitment to grid resiliency and long-term sustainability.
Financial Impact: Strategic investments in grid resiliency can reduce operational expenses, enhance revenue growth, and mitigate regulatory risks.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and customers value grid resiliency investments, as they enhance grid reliability, safety, and sustainability.

Description: Evaluates the potential impact of project development on water quality, considering factors such as water pollution, aquatic habitat disruption, and community water resources.
Calculation: Based on a standardized WQIA framework, incorporating data on water quality parameters, aquatic habitat assessment, and stakeholder engagement.
Relevance: Critical for assessing and mitigating the environmental risks associated with infrastructure projects, particularly those affecting water resources.
Financial Impact: Potential costs of water treatment, regulatory compliance, and reputational risks related to water quality impacts.
Stakeholder Perspective: Local communities, regulatory bodies, and investors concerned about environmental and social impacts.

Metric Name: Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Intensity of Project Development
Description: Measures the GHG emissions associated with project development, normalized by project value. This metric helps assess the carbon footprint of infrastructure projects.
Calculation: Total GHG emissions (t CO2e) / Total project value ($ million)
Relevance: Essential for understanding the climate-related risks and opportunities associated with infrastructure projects, particularly in the context of transition to a low-carbon economy.
Financial Impact: Potential costs of carbon pricing, regulatory compliance, and reputational risks related to climate change.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors focused on climate-related risks and opportunities, regulatory bodies, and stakeholders concerned about sustainability.

Description: Evaluates the level of engagement with local communities affected by project development, considering factors such as public consultations, information sharing, and grievance mechanisms.
Calculation: (Number of engaged community members / Total community members) x 100
Relevance: Critical for ensuring that infrastructure projects are socially responsible, minimize adverse impacts on local communities, and foster positive relationships.
Financial Impact: Potential costs of community relations, regulatory compliance, and reputational risks related to social impacts.
Stakeholder Perspective: Local communities, regulatory bodies, and investors concerned about social and environmental impacts.

Description: Measures the proportion of recycled materials used in project development, considering factors such as material sourcing, waste reduction, and recycling practices.
Calculation: (Quantity of recycled materials used / Total materials used) x 100
Relevance: Essential for reducing waste, conserving natural resources, and promoting sustainable practices in infrastructure project development.
Financial Impact: Potential cost savings from reduced material procurement, waste management, and regulatory compliance.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors focused on sustainability, regulatory bodies, and stakeholders concerned about environmental impacts.

Unit: Hectares of offset habitat per hectare of impacted habitat
Description: Evaluates the effectiveness of biodiversity offset measures implemented to mitigate the impacts of project development on ecosystems and biodiversity.
Calculation: Total area of offset habitat / Total area of impacted habitat
Relevance: Critical for ensuring that infrastructure projects minimize adverse impacts on biodiversity and ecosystems, and implement effective offset measures.
Financial Impact: Potential costs of biodiversity offset measures, regulatory compliance, and reputational risks related to environmental damage.
Stakeholder Perspective: Environmental groups, regulatory bodies, and investors focused on sustainability and environmental stewardship.

Description: Measures the frequency of environmental incidents associated with project development, such as spills, leaks, or other environmental releases.
Calculation: Total number of environmental incidents / Total number of projects
Relevance: Essential for understanding the environmental risks associated with infrastructure projects and implementing measures to prevent incidents.
Financial Impact: Potential costs of incident response, regulatory compliance, and reputational risks related to environmental damage.
Stakeholder Perspective: Regulatory bodies, investors focused on sustainability, and stakeholders concerned about environmental impacts.

Unit: Percentage of suppliers engaged on sustainability
Description: Evaluates the level of engagement with suppliers on sustainability issues, considering factors such as environmental and social performance, certification schemes, and capacity building.
Calculation: (Number of suppliers engaged on sustainability / Total suppliers) x 100
Relevance: Critical for promoting sustainable practices throughout the supply chain, reducing risks, and fostering positive relationships with stakeholders.
Financial Impact: Potential cost savings from reduced supply chain risks, improved supplier performance, and reputational benefits.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors focused on sustainability, regulatory bodies, and stakeholders concerned about environmental and social impacts.

Description: Tracks the frequency of safety incidents, including injuries and fatalities, during construction projects, reflecting the sector's commitment to worker safety.
Calculation: (Number of safety incidents / Total work hours) x 200,000
Relevance: Critical for evaluating the effectiveness of safety protocols and management systems, influencing operational efficiency and worker well-being.
Financial Impact: Direct costs of incidents, workers' compensation claims, and potential fines; indirect costs from decreased productivity and reputational damage.
Stakeholder Perspective: Regulators, investors, and employees focus on SIR as a key indicator of the sector's safety culture and operational excellence.

Description: Measures the frequency of design errors or omissions in construction projects, indicating potential risks to structural integrity and project timelines.
Calculation: (Number of design errors / Total design documents) x 100
Relevance: Important for assessing the sector's design quality and attention to detail, influencing project delivery and client satisfaction.
Financial Impact: Costs associated with design rework, delays, and potential claims; reputational damage from failed projects.
Stakeholder Perspective: Clients and investors prioritize design quality to ensure project success and minimize risk.

Description: Tracks the frequency of non-conforming materials used in construction projects, reflecting the sector's commitment to quality and safety standards.
Calculation: (Number of non-conforming materials / Total materials inspected) x 1,000
Relevance: Essential for ensuring compliance with regulatory requirements and industry standards, influencing structural integrity and project quality.
Financial Impact: Costs associated with material replacement, rework, and potential claims; reputational damage from compromised quality.
Stakeholder Perspective: Regulators, clients, and investors prioritize material quality to ensure structural integrity and project success.

Description: Measures the frequency of construction defects or deficiencies in completed projects, indicating potential risks to client satisfaction and asset value.
Calculation: (Number of construction defects / Total completed projects) x 100
Relevance: Important for evaluating the sector's construction quality and attention to detail, influencing client satisfaction and reputation.
Financial Impact: Costs associated with defect rectification, warranty claims, and potential litigation; reputational damage from compromised quality.
Stakeholder Perspective: Clients and investors prioritize construction quality to ensure asset value and minimize risk.

Description: Tracks the percentage of projects completed within budget, reflecting the sector's ability to manage costs and deliver projects efficiently.
Calculation: (Number of projects completed within budget / Total projects) x 100
Relevance: Essential for evaluating the sector's cost management and project delivery capabilities, influencing profitability and client satisfaction.
Financial Impact: Direct costs associated with cost overruns; indirect costs from reputational damage and decreased client trust.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors and clients prioritize project delivery within budget to ensure cost-effectiveness and minimize risk.

Description: Measures the percentage of structures equipped with SHM systems, indicating the sector's commitment to proactive maintenance and risk management.
Calculation: (Number of structures with SHM systems / Total structures) x 100
Relevance: Important for evaluating the sector's ability to identify potential structural issues and mitigate risks, influencing asset value and client satisfaction.
Financial Impact: Costs associated with SHM system installation and maintenance; potential cost savings from early defect detection and prevention.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and clients prioritize SHM coverage to ensure structural integrity and minimize risk.

Unit: Safety investment as a percentage of total project costs
Description: Tracks the sector's investment in safety initiatives, training, and technologies as a percentage of total project costs, reflecting its commitment to proactive safety management.
Calculation: (Safety investment / Total project costs) x 100
Relevance: Essential for evaluating the sector's proactive approach to safety management, influencing operational efficiency and worker well-being.
Financial Impact: Potential cost savings from reduced incidents and improved productivity; reputational benefits from demonstrating a strong safety culture.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and employees prioritize safety investment to ensure a safe working environment and minimize risk.

Metric Name: Health and Wellness Program Participation Rate
Description: Tracks the percentage of employees participating in health and wellness programs, indicating the effectiveness of initiatives promoting employee well-being.
Calculation: (Number of employees participating in health and wellness programs / Total number of employees) x 100
Relevance: Demonstrates the company's commitment to employee health and well-being, influencing employee engagement and retention.
Financial Impact: Can lead to reduced healthcare costs, improved productivity, and lower turnover rates.
Stakeholder Perspective: Employees, investors, and customers value a healthy and engaged workforce.

Description: Measures the frequency of work-related incidents that require recording, including injuries and illnesses, to assess the overall health and safety performance.
Calculation: (Number of recordable incidents / Total work hours) x 200,000
Relevance: Essential for identifying areas for improvement and evaluating the effectiveness of health and safety protocols.
Financial Impact: Affects workers' compensation costs, productivity, and project timelines.
Stakeholder Perspective: Regulators, investors, and employees value a safe work environment and low incident rates.

Description: Tracks the percentage of employees who have completed required safety training and certification programs, ensuring a competent workforce.
Calculation: (Number of employees with completed safety training and certification / Total number of employees) x 100
Relevance: Demonstrates the company's commitment to employee safety and regulatory compliance.
Financial Impact: Can lead to reduced incident rates, improved productivity, and lower workers' compensation costs.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and employees value a well-trained and competent workforce.

Description: Measures employee perceptions of the company's safety culture, including communication, training, and incident reporting.
Calculation: Average score from employee surveys and feedback
Relevance: Influences employee engagement, retention, and overall health and safety performance.
Financial Impact: Can lead to improved productivity, reduced turnover rates, and lower incident rates.
Stakeholder Perspective: Employees, investors, and customers value a positive safety culture.

Description: Evaluates the maturity and effectiveness of the company's OH&S management system, including policies, procedures, and protocols.
Calculation: Average score from internal audits and assessments
Relevance: Essential for ensuring regulatory compliance, reducing risks, and improving health and safety performance.
Financial Impact: Can lead to reduced incident rates, improved productivity, and lower workers' compensation costs.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and employees value a robust OH&S management system.

Description: Tracks the percentage of employees who return to work after an injury or illness, highlighting the effectiveness of RTW programs.
Calculation: (Number of employees returned to work / Total number of employees with injuries or illnesses) x 100
Relevance: Influences employee retention, productivity, and overall health and safety performance.
Financial Impact: Can lead to reduced workers' compensation costs, improved productivity, and lower turnover rates.
Stakeholder Perspective: Employees, investors, and customers value a supportive work environment.

Description: Measures the company's investment in health and safety initiatives, including training, equipment, and programs, as a percentage of total operating expenses.
Calculation: (Health and safety expenditure / Total operating expenses) x 100
Relevance: Demonstrates the company's commitment to employee health and safety, influencing stakeholder perceptions and regulatory compliance.
Financial Impact: Can lead to reduced incident rates, improved productivity, and lower workers' compensation costs.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and employees value a proactive approach to health and safety.

Description: Tracks the proportion of sustainable materials used in construction projects, such as recycled materials, low-carbon concrete, or sustainably sourced timber. This metric assesses the company's commitment to reducing environmental impacts throughout the supply chain.
Calculation: (Quantity of sustainable materials used / Total quantity of materials used) × 100
Relevance: Sustainable materials sourcing reduces environmental impacts, supports regulatory compliance, and enhances brand reputation.
Financial Impact: Reduced material costs, lower regulatory compliance expenses, and enhanced brand reputation contribute to long-term financial benefits.
Stakeholder Perspective: Environmental groups, customers, and investors increasingly value sustainable materials sourcing as a key aspect of environmental stewardship.

Metric Name: Energy Efficiency in Buildings (Energy Use Intensity)
Description: Measures the energy consumption per unit area of buildings, reflecting the energy efficiency of building design, operations, and maintenance. This metric helps identify opportunities for energy savings and reduced greenhouse gas emissions.
Calculation: Total energy consumption (kWh) / Total building area (m²)
Relevance: Energy efficiency in buildings reduces operational costs, supports regulatory compliance, and enhances environmental performance.
Financial Impact: Reduced energy costs, lower greenhouse gas emissions, and enhanced regulatory compliance contribute to cost savings and improved financial performance.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, customers, and regulatory bodies focus on energy efficiency as a key indicator of environmental performance and operational efficiency.

Description: Tracks the water consumption per unit area of construction projects, reflecting the effectiveness of water conservation measures during construction. This metric supports reduced water usage and environmental impacts.
Calculation: Total water consumption (liters) / Total construction area (m²)
Relevance: Water conservation during construction reduces environmental impacts, supports regulatory compliance, and enhances brand reputation.
Financial Impact: Reduced water costs, lower regulatory compliance expenses, and enhanced brand reputation contribute to long-term financial benefits.
Stakeholder Perspective: Environmental groups, customers, and investors value water conservation as a key aspect of environmental stewardship.

Description: Measures the proportion of assets requiring maintenance or repair, reflecting the effectiveness of asset management practices. A lower backlog indicates proactive maintenance and reduced risk of asset failure.
Calculation: (Number of assets requiring maintenance / Total number of assets) × 100
Relevance: Effective asset maintenance reduces the risk of asset failure, supports operational efficiency, and enhances safety.
Financial Impact: Reduced maintenance costs, lower risk of asset failure, and enhanced operational efficiency contribute to cost savings and improved financial performance.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, customers, and regulatory bodies focus on asset maintenance as a key indicator of operational efficiency and risk management.

Description: Tracks the proportion of suppliers assessed for environmental, social, and governance (ESG) risks, reflecting the company's commitment to responsible supply chain management.
Calculation: (Number of suppliers assessed / Total number of suppliers) × 100
Relevance: Supply chain risk assessment supports responsible sourcing, reduces reputational risk, and enhances brand reputation.
Financial Impact: Reduced reputational risk, improved supply chain resilience, and enhanced brand reputation contribute to long-term financial benefits.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, customers, and environmental groups value supply chain risk assessment as a key aspect of responsible business practices.

Description: Measures the company's ability to design, build, and maintain resilient buildings and infrastructure that can adapt to changing environmental conditions, such as climate change.
Calculation: Composite index score based on factors such as design for resilience, materials selection, and adaptability to changing conditions
Relevance: Building resilience and adaptation support reduced risk of asset failure, enhanced operational efficiency, and improved environmental performance.
Financial Impact: Reduced risk of asset failure, lower insurance costs, and enhanced regulatory compliance contribute to cost savings and improved financial performance.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, customers, and regulatory bodies focus on building resilience and adaptation as a key indicator of environmental performance and risk management.

Metric Name: Circular Economy in Construction (Material Reuse and Recycling Rate)
Description: Tracks the proportion of materials reused or recycled in construction projects, reflecting the company's commitment to circular economy principles and waste reduction.
Calculation: (Quantity of reused or recycled materials / Total quantity of materials used) × 100
Relevance: Circular economy practices reduce waste, support regulatory compliance, and enhance brand reputation.
Financial Impact: Reduced waste disposal costs, lower material costs, and enhanced brand reputation contribute to long-term financial benefits.
Stakeholder Perspective: Environmental groups, customers, and investors increasingly value circular economy practices as a key aspect of environmental stewardship and sustainable development.

Metric Name: Renewable Energy Percentage in New Projects
Description: Tracks the percentage of new projects that incorporate renewable energy sources, indicating the company's commitment to a low-carbon transition.
Calculation: (Number of new projects with renewable energy / Total new projects) × 100
Relevance: Demonstrates the company's strategic shift towards low-carbon projects and climate resilience.
Financial Impact: Influences long-term cost stability, regulatory compliance, and revenue growth from low-carbon projects.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, customers, and environmental groups value the company's commitment to renewable energy.

Description: Measures the percentage of projects designed with climate-resilient features, such as flood protection or heat mitigation measures.
Calculation: (Number of projects with climate-resilient design / Total projects) × 100
Relevance: Essential for ensuring that projects can withstand climate-related risks and maintain their value over time.
Financial Impact: Reduces potential losses from climate-related events and enhances asset resilience.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, customers, and regulatory bodies focus on climate resilience as a key indicator of long-term viability.

Description: Quantifies the greenhouse gas emissions associated with the company's supply chain, highlighting opportunities for reduction.
Calculation: Total GHG emissions (tCO2e) from supply chain activities
Relevance: Critical for understanding and managing climate-related risks and opportunities in the supply chain.
Financial Impact: Affects costs associated with supplier engagement, logistics, and procurement.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, customers, and sustainability-focused stakeholders value transparency and action on supply chain carbon footprint.

Description: Tracks the percentage of projects that achieve green building certifications, such as LEED or BREEAM, indicating a commitment to sustainable design and operations.
Calculation: (Number of certified projects / Total projects) × 100
Relevance: Demonstrates the company's focus on sustainable buildings and reduced environmental impact.
Financial Impact: Influences revenue growth from green building projects, cost savings from energy efficiency, and enhanced brand reputation.
Stakeholder Perspective: Customers, investors, and environmental groups value green building certifications as a symbol of sustainability leadership.

Description: Measures the company's investment in climate change adaptation measures, such as climate-resilient infrastructure or climate-smart design.
Calculation: Total investment in climate change adaptation measures (million USD)
Relevance: Essential for demonstrating the company's proactive approach to managing climate-related risks and opportunities.
Financial Impact: Directly affects costs associated with climate change adaptation and long-term asset resilience.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulatory bodies, and stakeholders value the company's commitment to climate change adaptation.

Description: Tracks the reduction in greenhouse gas emissions achieved through specific projects or initiatives, highlighting the company's climate performance.
Calculation: Total GHG emissions reductions (tCO2e) from projects
Relevance: Critical for evaluating the effectiveness of the company's climate-related projects and initiatives.
Financial Impact: Influences costs associated with carbon pricing, regulatory compliance, and reputational benefits.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, customers, and sustainability-focused stakeholders value tangible GHG emissions reductions.

Description: Measures the percentage of the company's project portfolio that has undergone a forward-looking climate risk assessment, indicating preparedness for climate-related risks.
Calculation: (Number of projects with climate risk assessment / Total projects) × 100
Relevance: Essential for identifying and managing climate-related risks and opportunities in the company's project portfolio.
Financial Impact: Directly affects costs associated with climate-related risk management and long-term asset resilience.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulatory bodies, and stakeholders value the company's proactive approach to climate risk management.

Description: Measures the percentage of employees who have completed anti-corruption training within a specified timeframe (e.g., annually), indicating the company's commitment to preventing corruption.
Calculation: (Number of employees completed anti-corruption training / Total employees) × 100
Relevance: Essential for ensuring employees understand anti-corruption policies and procedures.
Financial Impact: Reduces risk of corruption-related fines, penalties, and reputational damage.
Stakeholder Perspective: Regulators, investors, and business partners expect companies to have effective anti-corruption measures in place.

Description: Measures the percentage of business partners assessed for ethics risks within a specified timeframe (e.g., annually), indicating the company's commitment to managing ethics risks throughout its supply chain.
Calculation: (Number of business partners assessed for ethics risks / Total business partners) × 100
Relevance: Critical for identifying and mitigating potential ethics risks associated with business partners.
Financial Impact: Effective risk assessment and management can prevent reputational damage, regulatory fines, and financial losses.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and customers expect companies to manage ethics risks throughout their supply chains.

Description: Measures the rate of ethics incidents (e.g., conflicts of interest, gifts and entertainment policy breaches) per 1,000 employees, indicating the company's effectiveness in promoting a strong ethics culture.
Calculation: (Number of ethics incidents / Total employees) × 1,000
Relevance: Essential for monitoring and managing ethics risks and promoting a strong ethics culture.
Financial Impact: Effective management of ethics incidents can mitigate reputational damage, regulatory fines, and litigation costs.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and employees value a company's commitment to promoting a strong ethics culture.

Description: Measures the percentage of audit committee meetings that include discussions on ethics and compliance topics, indicating the company's commitment to effective governance and oversight.
Calculation: (Number of audit committee meetings with ethics and compliance discussions / Total audit committee meetings) × 100
Relevance: Critical for ensuring effective governance and oversight of ethics and compliance risks.
Financial Impact: Effective oversight can mitigate reputational damage, regulatory fines, and financial losses.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors and regulators expect companies to have effective governance and oversight of ethics and compliance risks.

Description: Measures the percentage of employees who participate in ethics surveys, indicating the company's commitment to engaging employees on ethics topics and promoting a strong ethics culture.
Calculation: (Number of employees participated in ethics survey / Total employees) × 100
Relevance: Essential for understanding employee perceptions of the company's ethics culture and identifying areas for improvement.
Financial Impact: Effective employee engagement on ethics topics can promote a strong ethics culture and mitigate reputational damage.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and employees value a company's commitment to promoting a strong ethics culture.

Description: Measures the percentage of third-party relationships (e.g., suppliers, contractors) subject to due diligence assessments for ethics risks, indicating the company's commitment to managing ethics risks throughout its supply chain.
Calculation: (Number of third-party relationships assessed for ethics risks / Total third-party relationships) × 100
Relevance: Critical for identifying and mitigating potential ethics risks associated with third-party relationships.
Financial Impact: Effective due diligence can prevent reputational damage, regulatory fines, and financial losses.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and customers expect companies to manage ethics risks throughout their supply chains.

Description: Measures the maturity of the company's ethics and compliance program, including elements such as policies, procedures, training, and monitoring, indicating the company's commitment to effective ethics and compliance management.
Calculation: Based on a comprehensive assessment of the company's ethics and compliance program, using a scoring system (e.g., 1-5).
Relevance: Essential for ensuring effective ethics and compliance management and mitigating reputational damage, regulatory fines, and financial losses.
Financial Impact: Effective ethics and compliance management can prevent reputational damage, regulatory fines, and financial losses.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and business partners expect companies to have effective ethics and compliance programs in place.

Description: The percentage of eligible low-income customers participating in energy assistance programs, indicating the company's efforts to support vulnerable populations.
Calculation: (Number of participating low-income customers / Total eligible low-income customers) × 100
Relevance: This metric evaluates the company's initiatives to address energy poverty and support low-income households.
Financial Impact: Participation in energy assistance programs can reduce bad debt expenses and improve customer relationships.
Stakeholder Perspective: Low-income households, regulatory bodies, and investors focused on social responsibility.

Description: A measure of the volatility of gas prices, indicating the company's exposure to market risks and ability to manage price fluctuations.
Calculation: Standard deviation of monthly gas price changes over a 12-month period
Relevance: This metric assesses the company's risk management strategies and ability to maintain stable energy prices.
Financial Impact: Price volatility can impact revenue and profitability, while effective risk management can reduce costs.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, risk management teams, and regulatory bodies.

Description: The average annual savings per customer resulting from energy efficiency programs and initiatives.
Calculation: Total energy cost savings / Number of participating customers
Relevance: This metric evaluates the company's efforts to reduce energy costs for customers and promote energy efficiency.
Financial Impact: Energy efficiency programs can lead to increased customer satisfaction, reduced energy consumption, and new revenue streams.
Stakeholder Perspective: Customers, investors, and regulatory bodies focused on energy efficiency.

Description: The percentage of capital expenditures and operating expenses dedicated to initiatives supporting energy affordability, such as low-income assistance programs and energy efficiency projects.
Calculation: (Affordability-related investments / Total capital expenditures and operating expenses) × 100
Relevance: This metric assesses the company's commitment to energy affordability and investments in related initiatives.
Financial Impact: Strategic investments in energy affordability can lead to long-term cost savings, improved customer relationships, and increased revenue.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulatory bodies, and customers.

Description: The percentage of customers disconnected for non-payment, indicating the company's effectiveness in managing bad debt and supporting vulnerable customers.
Calculation: (Number of customers disconnected for non-payment / Total customers) × 100
Relevance: This metric evaluates the company's strategies for managing bad debt and supporting customers experiencing financial difficulties.
Financial Impact: High disconnection rates can lead to increased bad debt expenses and reputational damage.
Stakeholder Perspective: Low-income households, regulatory bodies, and investors focused on social responsibility.

Unit: Number of customers (or percentage of customer base)
Description: The number or percentage of customers participating in energy efficiency programs, indicating the company's efforts to promote energy savings and affordability.
Calculation: Number of customers participating in energy efficiency programs / Total customers
Relevance: This metric assesses the company's initiatives to support energy efficiency and reduce energy costs for customers.
Financial Impact: Energy efficiency programs can lead to increased customer satisfaction, reduced energy consumption, and new revenue streams.
Stakeholder Perspective: Customers, investors, and regulatory bodies focused on energy efficiency.

Description: A predictive metric assessing the company's expected performance on energy affordability over the next 12-18 months, based on factors such as planned investments, market trends, and regulatory developments.
Calculation: Weighted average of forecasted affordability metrics, including energy prices, customer assistance programs, and energy efficiency initiatives
Relevance: This metric provides forward-looking insights into the company's energy affordability performance and strategic direction.
Financial Impact: A strong forward-looking affordability index can indicate a company's potential for long-term financial stability and growth.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, executive management, and regulatory bodies.

Description: Measures the proportion of customers with smart meters installed, enabling real-time energy usage monitoring and efficiency opportunities.
Calculation: (Number of customers with smart meters) / (Total number of customers) × 100
Relevance: Critical for assessing the utility's readiness for a more efficient and responsive energy system.
Financial Impact: Supports cost savings through reduced meter reading and customer service costs, and enables more effective demand response and energy efficiency programs.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors and regulators focus on the utility's ability to modernize infrastructure and improve operational efficiency.

Unit: Percentage (%) reduction in average daily energy usage
Description: Tracks the reduction in average daily energy usage among customers participating in energy efficiency programs.
Calculation: [(Average daily energy usage before program participation) - (Average daily energy usage after program participation)] / (Average daily energy usage before program participation) × 100
Relevance: Directly measures the impact of energy efficiency programs on customer behavior and energy consumption.
Financial Impact: Affects revenue through reduced energy sales, but also provides opportunities for cost savings and regulatory compliance benefits.
Stakeholder Perspective: Customers, investors, and regulators value energy efficiency efforts as a means to reduce environmental impact and ensure sustainable energy supply.

Unit: Percentage (%) of leaks detected and repaired within a specified timeframe
Description: Measures the effectiveness of leak detection and repair programs in minimizing energy losses and ensuring system integrity.
Calculation: (Number of leaks detected and repaired) / (Total number of leaks detected) × 100
Relevance: Essential for evaluating the utility's ability to maintain system integrity and minimize energy losses.
Financial Impact: Directly affects revenue through reduced energy losses and costs associated with leak detection and repair.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and customers value the utility's ability to maintain a safe and reliable energy system.

Description: Tracks the investment in energy efficiency programs and initiatives aimed at reducing energy consumption.
Calculation: Total investment in energy efficiency programs
Relevance: Critical for evaluating the utility's commitment to energy efficiency and sustainability.
Financial Impact: Affects costs and revenue through reduced energy sales, but also provides opportunities for cost savings and regulatory compliance benefits.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and customers value energy efficiency efforts as a means to reduce environmental impact and ensure sustainable energy supply.

Description: Measures the level of customer engagement and participation in energy efficiency programs and initiatives.
Calculation: (Number of customers participating in energy efficiency programs) / (Total number of customers) × 100
Relevance: Essential for evaluating the effectiveness of energy efficiency programs and customer engagement strategies.
Financial Impact: Affects revenue through reduced energy sales, but also provides opportunities for cost savings and regulatory compliance benefits.
Stakeholder Perspective: Customers, investors, and regulators value energy efficiency efforts as a means to reduce environmental impact and ensure sustainable energy supply.

Description: Tracks the energy lost during transmission and distribution, reflecting the efficiency of the gas distribution system.
Calculation: (Energy lost during transmission and distribution) / (Total energy delivered to customers) × 100
Relevance: Critical for evaluating the utility's ability to maintain system integrity and minimize energy losses.
Financial Impact: Directly affects revenue through reduced energy sales and costs associated with energy losses.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and customers value the utility's ability to maintain a safe and reliable energy system.

Unit: Metric tons CO2e per therm delivered
Description: Measures the greenhouse gas emissions associated with delivering energy to customers, reflecting the utility's carbon footprint.
Calculation: (Greenhouse gas emissions from energy delivery) / (Total energy delivered to customers)
Relevance: Essential for evaluating the utility's environmental impact and commitment to sustainability.
Financial Impact: Affects costs and revenue through carbon pricing and regulatory compliance benefits.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulators, and customers value the utility's commitment to reducing greenhouse gas emissions and ensuring a sustainable energy supply.

Description: Measures the average time taken to repair pipeline leaks or damages, reflecting operational efficiency and responsiveness to incidents.
Calculation: Total downtime hours for repairs / Number of repairs
Relevance: Impacts operational efficiency, safety, and customer satisfaction.
Financial Impact: Affects costs associated with repair activities, lost revenue during downtime, and potential penalties for delayed repairs.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors and customers value quick response times to minimize disruptions and ensure reliability.

Description: Measures the frequency of gas leaks per unit of pipeline length, indicating the effectiveness of leak detection and prevention measures.
Calculation: (Number of gas leaks / Total pipeline length in miles) × 100
Relevance: Critical for assessing operational safety, environmental impact, and regulatory compliance.
Financial Impact: Directly affects costs associated with leak detection, repair, and potential environmental liabilities.
Stakeholder Perspective: Environmental groups, regulators, and investors prioritize low leak rates for safety and sustainability.

Description: Measures the percentage of assets (pipelines, facilities) under active management, reflecting the effectiveness of asset maintenance and renewal programs.
Calculation: (Assets under active management / Total assets) × 100
Relevance: Essential for ensuring asset reliability, optimizing maintenance costs, and supporting long-term strategic planning.
Financial Impact: Affects capital expenditures, operating expenses, and asset valuation.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors and regulators value effective asset management for long-term sustainability.

Description: Measures the average response time to emergency situations (e.g., gas leaks, pipeline ruptures), reflecting operational preparedness and responsiveness.
Calculation: Total response time for emergency incidents / Number of incidents
Relevance: Critical for ensuring public safety, minimizing incident impacts, and regulatory compliance.
Financial Impact: Affects costs associated with emergency response, potential liabilities from incidents, and reputation.
Stakeholder Perspective: Regulators, customers, and investors prioritize quick emergency response times for safety and reliability.

Description: Measures the percentage of pipeline and facility assets receiving regular preventive maintenance, reflecting proactive risk management.
Calculation: (Assets receiving preventive maintenance / Total assets) × 100
Relevance: Essential for minimizing operational risks, optimizing maintenance costs, and ensuring asset reliability.
Financial Impact: Affects maintenance costs, asset lifespan, and potential costs from unplanned repairs.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors and regulators value proactive maintenance practices for safety and cost-effectiveness.

Description: Measures the percentage of capital expenditures allocated to infrastructure upgrades, replacements, and expansions, reflecting strategic investment in asset renewal.
Calculation: (Infrastructure investment / Total capital expenditures) × 100
Relevance: Critical for ensuring long-term asset reliability, supporting growth, and regulatory compliance.
Financial Impact: Affects capital expenditures, asset valuation, and potential returns on investment.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors and regulators prioritize strategic infrastructure investments for long-term sustainability.

Description: Measures the percentage of gas delivery interruptions or outages below a certain threshold (e.g., 5 minutes), reflecting operational reliability and customer satisfaction.
Calculation: (Number of interruptions below threshold / Total number of interruptions) × 100
Relevance: Essential for ensuring customer satisfaction, regulatory compliance, and minimizing revenue impacts from outages.
Financial Impact: Affects revenue, customer retention, and potential penalties for service disruptions.
Stakeholder Perspective: Customers, investors, and regulators prioritize high reliability for service quality and trust.

Description: Tracks the rate at which the company acquires land for conservation purposes, either through purchase or conservation easements. This metric demonstrates the company's commitment to mitigating ecological impacts.
Calculation: Total hectares of land acquired for conservation / Year
Relevance: Indicates proactive efforts to protect natural habitats and ecosystems affected by home building activities.
Financial Impact: Affects long-term costs associated with land management, conservation, and potential revenue from eco-tourism or carbon credits.
Stakeholder Perspective: Environmental organizations, local communities, and investors interested in sustainability performance.

Description: Measures the net gain in biodiversity value resulting from conservation efforts compared to the impacts of land development. This metric assesses the effectiveness of ecological restoration initiatives.
Calculation: (Biodiversity value after conservation - Biodiversity value before development) / Biodiversity value before development
Relevance: Critical for evaluating the success of ecological mitigation and restoration measures.
Financial Impact: Influences costs associated with habitat restoration, regulatory compliance, and potential revenue from biodiversity offsets.
Stakeholder Perspective: Environmental stakeholders, regulatory agencies, and investors focused on ecological performance.

Description: Estimates the monetary value of ecosystem services provided by natural habitats, such as carbon sequestration, water filtration, and soil formation. This metric helps quantify the economic benefits of conservation.
Calculation: Use established ecosystem services valuation methodologies (e.g., InVEST, ARIES) to estimate the monetary value of ecosystem services.
Relevance: Essential for understanding the economic benefits of ecological conservation and restoration efforts.
Financial Impact: Directly affects costs associated with environmental compliance, habitat restoration, and potential revenue from ecosystem services.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, regulatory bodies, and stakeholders interested in the economic value of ecological conservation.

Description: Measures the efficiency of land use in home building projects, considering the proportion of developable land versus total land area. This metric assesses operational efficiency and ecological impact.
Calculation: (Developable land area / Total land area) × 100
Relevance: Critical for optimizing land use, minimizing ecological impacts, and maximizing development potential.
Financial Impact: Affects costs associated with land acquisition, development, and potential revenue from property sales.
Stakeholder Perspective: Investors, executive management, and stakeholders interested in operational efficiency and sustainability performance.

Description: Tracks the rate at which the company restores or rehabilitates degraded or converted habitats. This metric demonstrates the company's commitment to ecological conservation.
Calculation: Total hectares of land restored or rehabilitated / Year
Relevance: Essential for understanding the company's efforts to mitigate ecological impacts and promote biodiversity.
Financial Impact: Affects costs associated with habitat restoration, regulatory compliance, and potential revenue from eco-tourism or carbon credits.
Stakeholder Perspective: Environmental organizations, regulatory agencies, and investors focused on sustainability performance.

Description: Measures the proportion of land under conservation easements, which restrict development and protect natural habitats. This metric assesses the company's commitment to long-term ecological conservation.
Calculation: (Land area under conservation easements / Total land area) × 100
Relevance: Critical for ensuring the long-term protection of natural habitats and ecosystems.
Financial Impact: Affects costs associated with land management, conservation, and potential revenue from eco-tourism or carbon credits.
Stakeholder Perspective: Environmental stakeholders, regulatory agencies, and investors focused on sustainability performance.

Description: Tracks the proportion of home building projects that undergo comprehensive ecological impact assessments. This metric ensures that ecological considerations are integrated into project planning and decision-making.
Calculation: (Number of projects with PEIA / Total number of projects) × 100
Relevance: Essential for identifying and mitigating ecological impacts at the project level.
Financial Impact: Directly affects costs associated with environmental compliance, habitat restoration, and potential regulatory fines.
Stakeholder Perspective: Environmental stakeholders, regulatory agencies, and investors focused on sustainability performance and risk management.

Metric Name: Employee Training Hours per Construction Site
Description: Tracks the investment in employee training and development, ensuring workers have necessary skills to perform tasks safely and efficiently.
Calculation: Total training hours / Number of construction sites
Relevance: Enhances workforce competency, reduces errors, and promotes a safety-first culture.
Financial Impact: Inadequate training can lead to costly mistakes, rework, and accidents, while effective training improves productivity and reduces risks.
Stakeholder Perspective: Important for investors, regulators, and sustainability-focused stakeholders

Metric Name: Workforce Health and Safety Incident Rate by Job Function
Description: Identifies high-risk job functions and areas where targeted interventions can prevent incidents and improve overall health and safety performance.
Calculation: (Number of incidents by job function / Number of employees in that function) x 100
Relevance: Enables data-driven decision-making to allocate resources effectively and prioritize safety initiatives.
Financial Impact: Reduces workers' compensation claims, medical costs, and lost productivity associated with job-specific hazards.
Stakeholder Perspective: Important for investors, regulators, and sustainability-focused stakeholders

Metric Name: Return to Work (RTW) Rate after Injury
Description: Measures the effectiveness of return-to-work programs, supporting injured employees' recovery and reintegration into the workforce.
Calculation: (Number of employees returned to work / Total number of injured employees) x 100
Relevance: Impacts employee well-being, retention, and productivity, while reducing workers' compensation costs and liabilities.
Financial Impact: Impacts operational costs, regulatory compliance, and stakeholder value
Stakeholder Perspective: Important for investors, regulators, and sustainability-focused stakeholders

Description: Tracks adherence to regulatory requirements, industry standards, and company policies, ensuring a safe work environment.
Calculation: (Number of compliant sites / Total number of sites) x 100
Relevance: Essential for avoiding fines, reputational damage, and regulatory issues.
Financial Impact: Non-compliance can result in costly fines, penalties, and litigation.
Stakeholder Perspective: Important for investors, regulators, and sustainability-focused stakeholders

Metric Name: Employee Engagement and Safety Perception Index
Description: Gauges employee perceptions of health and safety practices, culture, and leadership commitment, driving continuous improvement.
Calculation: Average score from employee surveys and feedback
Relevance: Influences employee satisfaction, retention, and productivity, while informing safety strategy and initiatives.
Financial Impact: Impacts operational costs, regulatory compliance, and stakeholder value
Stakeholder Perspective: Important for investors, regulators, and sustainability-focused stakeholders

Metric Name: Near Miss and Incident Reporting Rate
Description: Encourages a culture of transparency and proactive risk management by tracking near misses and incidents.
Calculation: (Number of reports / Number of employees) x 100
